unit.title: Your first investment
unit.description: Buy your first share, understand why it moves and why investing early changes everything

texts: 40 years of stock market in 20 seconds
The **S&P 500** brings together the 500 largest US companies, like Apple and Amazon. You invest **€1,000** of virtual money in January 1985 and live through what really happened.
Without adding a single euro, how much is that €1,000 worth at the end of 2025?
About €2,000
About €8,000
More than €30,000
It's worth **€38,109**: about 38 times what you put in, not counting dividends or the exchange rate.
Get to 2025. If you get scared, you can sell.

There were two falls of around half (2000-2002 and 2008), and even so whoever didn't sell multiplied their money **38** times. Whoever started in 2005, only **5.8** times: **starting early** matters enormously.
You've sold. Look at what it would be worth if you'd held on.
Forty years, several crises and about 38 times your money.
Already over €11,000. All you had to do was wait.
Hit start. You can sell whenever you want.
I'll start when I earn more
Leo
Leo is 20 and has just seen that same chart.
Mind-blowing. But right now I can only put aside €50 a month.
Better to wait until I'm 30 and put in €100 a month.
Up to age 60 and earning 7 % a year, when does he end up with more?
If he starts now, with €50 a month
Exactly: he puts in €24,000 and gets to over €120,000.
If he waits, he puts in €36,000 and gets to about €117,000.
If he waits until 30, with €100 a month
With €36,000 in, he gets to about €117,000. Starting now, over €120,000.
More or less the same
Close, but starting now he puts in €12,000 less and ends up with more.
It's **compound interest**: what you earn also earns, and time multiplies it.
The 7 % is an example: the stock market promises nothing in any given year.
And how do I start without risking my money?
With virtual money, right here. I'll show you.

steps.title: What you've just discovered
steps.body:
• A **share** is a tiny piece of a company. With the S&P 500 you own a tiny piece of 500 at once.
• The stock market sometimes falls, and hard, but over those 40 years whoever didn't sell multiplied their money. That doesn't guarantee it will happen again.
• **Starting early** matters more than starting big.

In E-Trading you practise with virtual money: you can make mistakes without losing anything real.
steps.key: Investing means buying tiny pieces of companies and giving them time to grow.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for a company you know and buy your first share.

texts: Am I a bit of an owner now?
Sara
I've bought a share in a video game company.
Does that mean I'm already a bit of an owner?
What do you tell Sara?
Yes: of a tiny part of the business
Exactly. If the business does well you notice, and if it does badly, you do too.
No: it's just a number that goes up and down
Behind the price there's a real business, and you own a tiny slice.
Yes, and now she can run the company
She can vote at the shareholders' meeting, but her vote counts for very little.
So how do I make money from it?
In two ways: **dividends** (it shares out profits) and **capital gains** (the price rises).
In the long run, the price follows profits; in the short run, expectations.
If the company goes bust, shareholders get paid last and almost never get anything back.
Owner or lender?
Inditex has around 3,100 million **shares**: with one you own a tiny slice. With a **bond**, on the other hand, you lend it money.
Share: owner
Bond: lender
You own part of its shops, brands and profits
That's being a co-owner: equities (variable income).
You receive an agreed coupon
The bondholder gets what was agreed if the company can pay.
You get your money back on a set date
A bond matures; a share has no maturity date.
You receive dividends if the company pays them
A dividend is part of the profit that's paid out to the owners.
If the company goes bust, you get paid last
Creditors get paid first; shareholders almost never get anything back.
You make a lot if the business grows a lot
Shareholders share in the business's success and its risk.
Sort the six cards.
A share is **variable income**: what you make isn't fixed, it depends on how the business does. The bondholder, on the other hand, gets what was agreed.
Hint: the owner shares success and risk; the lender gets what was agreed.
More risk for the owner, but also more reward.
Tap each card: owner or lender?
Just one share
Real data: **€10,000** in Tesla at the end of 2018, measured in dollars and without dividends. This is what equities feel like.
Make it to the end, whether you sell or not.

Tesla multiplied almost 19 times over, but it fell as much as **72 %**, and it's an exception: just **4 %** of US stocks generated all of the market's net gain between 1926 and 2016. Try it: in Market, open Tesla and look at its 52-week range: the lowest and the highest.
You've sold. Watch what happens next…
30 % below what you put in. Can you hold on?
You've more than doubled your money. What if it falls now?
Hit «Start». You can sell whenever you like
The order book
You want 600 shares right now and the cheapest seller is asking **€10.04**. This is the **order book**: on the left, people who want to buy (*bid*); on the right, people who want to sell (*ask*).
You want to buy **600 shares** right now. What average price do you pay?
€10.04, the best selling price
A bit more than €10.04
€10.02, the best buying price
There are only 300 at €10.04: the other 300 cost €10.05. You pay €6,027, an average of **€10.045**.
Buy so many that your average price ends up more than 0.1 % away from the best price.
The difference between the best *bid* and the best *ask* is the **spread**. If more buyers in a hurry turn up, **they eat through the offers step by step** and the price rises.
Your own purchase has pushed the price up. That's how it moves.
The €10.04 shares are gone: the next ones cost more.
Change how many shares you buy at once
Surprise results
Leo
It's 10:00. The company Leo has invested in announces it has earned far more than expected.
In the book, the best seller was asking €10.04. What now?
What do you think happens to the price?
It rises: buyers eat through the offers
Exactly. The €10.04 shares run out, it trades at €10.05… and up it goes.
Nothing: the company sets the price
The company doesn't set the price: it's the last deal between a buyer and a seller.
It only depends on what the company is worth
That matters in the long run. Today, whoever's most eager to buy calls the shots.
So is the price what the company is worth?
No: it's what someone **has just paid**. News, results and data move it.

steps.title: What moves the price
steps.body:
The price you see isn't what the company is worth: it's what someone **has just paid**. If more buyers arrive in a hurry, it rises; if more sellers arrive, it falls.

The Madrid Stock Exchange opens and closes with an **auction**: from 8:30 to 9:00 and from 17:30 to 17:35 orders are gathered and a single price is set, the one that allows the most trades.
steps.key: The price is the latest deal between whoever pays most and whoever asks least.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open Inditex and see how much it has gone up or down today.

texts: Buy right now
You want shares in a small company that hardly trades and you tap «buy now». That's a **market order**: it buys instantly, at the best selling price there is.
You buy **1,000 shares at market**. What do you think will happen to your price?
You pay €4.00, the best price
You pay quite a bit more on average
You pay less: you're buying in bulk
There are only 200 at €4.00. Your 1,000 cost an average of **€4.115**: almost 3 % more.
Raise the purchase to 1,000 shares.
A market order **guarantees execution, not the price**. With illiquid securities, your order eats through several steps of the book.
Over 2 % extra, just for buying in a hurry.
The €4.00 shares are gone: now you're paying more.
Raise the quantity and watch your average price
Fast or cheap
Laura
I want 5,000 shares in a company that hardly trades.
I just hit «buy at market» and that's it, right?
What do you advise her?
Yes: at market you pay the price you see
At market you secure execution, not the price. Here she'd pay a lot more.
Better an order with her maximum price
That's it: a **limit order**. It buys up to her price and, if there are no sellers, it waits.
At market, but in several goes
It helps a little, but she still doesn't control the price.
With big companies during normal hours, the difference is usually a matter of cents.

steps.title: When it gets expensive
steps.body:
• **Illiquid securities** (ones almost nobody buys or sells): your order eats through several steps of the book.
• **The open, or right after news:** prices jump.
• **Exchange closed:** it'll execute at the open, at whatever the price is then.

In the simulator, a market buy goes in at the last price; at a real broker you would pay a little more (the spread). Before buying, also think about your **stop**: the price at which you'd sell to cut your loss if it falls.
steps.key: Market order = guaranteed speed, no guaranteed price.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, buy a big company at market and see what price you get in at.

texts: What does a chart tell you?

A friend shows you a share that keeps going up: «Should I buy now?». On its chart, **time** runs across, **price** up the side and **volume** (how much is traded) underneath: what does it tell you, and what doesn't it?
The chart shows it
It doesn't
What price it opened at yesterday
Every candle, the little bar for each day, records its open.
Tomorrow's price
Nobody knows: the chart is a record of the past.
The highest price of the week
Every candle records its high and its low.
How much was traded today
That's the volume: the bars at the bottom.
Whether the company is a good business
Its accounts tell you that, not its chart.
The close a year ago
The horizontal axis takes you back in time.
Whether it'll keep rising
It may or may not: these are probabilities, never certainties.
Sort the seven questions.
A chart is the **exact record** of what buyers and sellers agreed. It tells you what happened, **not what's going to happen**.
Has it already happened, or not yet? That's the key.
Can you read it on the chart?
Reading isn't guessing
Each little bar on the chart is a **candle**: what the price did in one day. Here are three real charts of 30 candles. Read them and decide: does it go **up or down** over the next 10 sessions?
Play all three rounds.
Reading the past is easy; guessing the future isn't. People who study charts work with **probabilities, never certainties**.
Three out of three! With so few rounds, luck plays a big part.
Calling the future with candles is hard for everyone.
Look at the candles and choose: up or down?

steps.title: Four prices per period
steps.body:
Each **candle** sums up a period (a day, a week…) with four figures (**OHLC**):

• **Open:** the first price.
• **High** and **low**.
• **Close:** the last one, and the most important.

In E-Trading, when you run your finger over a candle you see its four prices, the change and the volume. Reading a chart properly is already an advantage: lots of people only check whether it's green or red.
steps.key: A chart tells you what happened, not what's going to happen.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open Microsoft, switch the chart to candles and run your finger over the last one.

texts: The mattress, simple and compound

You have **€1,000** and 30 years ahead of you. Three ways to keep it:

• **Under the mattress:** it doesn't grow.
• **Simple interest:** you always earn on what you put in.
• **Compound interest:** you also earn on what you've already earned.
€1,000 at 7 % a year for 30 years. How much will you have with compound interest?
About €3,100
About €7,600
About €21,000
With simple interest it would be €3,100. With compound, **€7,612**: almost two and a half times as much, without adding a single euro.
Reach €10,000 without adding any money: play with the return (what your money earns each year) and the years.
Compounding **speeds up**: the last years grow much more than the first ones. That's why time matters as much as the return.
That much isn't normal: 7 % a year is already a lot over the long term.
Look at the end of the green curve: it shoots up!
Move the years: watch how the lines pull apart
Ana and Bruno
Both put aside **€200 a month** at 7 % until 65. Ana starts at 25. What if Bruno starts later?
Ana
Bruno
Bruno starts 10 years after Ana. At 65, how much will he have compared with her?
25 % less
Less than half
Almost the same
Ana ends up with about **€494,000** and Bruno with about **€234,000**: less than half, even though Ana only put in €24,000 more.
Delay Bruno until Ana has three times as much as him.
Every year you wait costs far more than it seems: your first euros are the ones with the most time to compound.
Starting at 45, Bruno can't catch up with Ana even if he puts in the same.
If they start at the same time, they end up the same. Now delay Bruno
Every year of delay widens the gap. How far does it go?

steps.title: It works against you too
steps.body:
Compound interest works the same way with debt: if a card charges you interest on interest and you don't pay it off, what you owe grows even if you buy nothing else.

And remember: these are examples, not promises. The stock market doesn't return 7 % every year.
steps.key: Gains generate new gains: the sooner you start, the more time works for you.
steps.tip: Try it: open Portfolio and see how much your first share has changed since you bought it.

h1l1-1.prompt: What are you buying when you buy a share?
options: One of the company's products at a discount
A small piece of the company
A loan to the company
h1l1-1.explanation: A share is a part of the company: you gain if the company is worth more, not because it owes you anything.

h1l1-2.prompt: You've put €1,000 of virtual money into the S&P 500 and within a few months it drops to €700. You won't need that money for years. What do you do?
options: Take out a loan to buy more while it's cheap
Hold on: I don't need it and I have time
Sell everything so I don't lose more
h1l1-2.explanation: Falls are part of investing. If you don't need the money, selling in the middle of a fall is what turns a temporary drop into a real loss.
feedback: If it keeps falling, you lose with money that isn't yours and you also owe the interest.
You give it time to recover. In 2008 it fell by more than half, and those who held on ended up multiplying their money.
By selling you turn a drop into a real loss, and you miss the recovery.

h1l1-3.prompt: Lumi thinks investing in the stock market is like going to a casino. What do you reply?
options: Only if you pick the right company
No: you buy tiny pieces of companies
Yes, it's pure luck: some days you win, some you lose
h1l1-3.explanation: In a casino the odds are set up for you to lose. On the stock market you buy parts of businesses that make profits, and with time and many companies at once the result depends much less on luck.
feedback: Picking well helps, but with 500 companies at once you no longer depend on getting one right.
Exactly. Behind every share there's a real business, not a roulette wheel.
In a casino the house always wins. A company that makes money tends to be worth more over the years.
lines: Investing in the stock market is like going to a casino, right?
Either you win it all or you lose it all.

h1l1-4.prompt: Does it help your money in the long run or hold it back?
options: Selling everything as soon as the market falls
Spreading it across many companies
Waiting until you have lots of money to start
Letting the years go by without touching it
Starting early, even with a little
h1l1-4.explanation: Time and spreading out work in your favour. Waiting or selling out of fear means time works less for you.

h1l1-5.prompt: Between 1985 and 2025, the S&P 500 never fell more than 20 %.
options: True
False
h1l1-5.explanation: It fell by almost half in 2000-2002 and by more than half in 2008-2009. Even so, whoever didn't sell multiplied their money 38 times: big falls pass, and holding on is the hard part.

h1l1-6.prompt: €1,000 in the S&P 500 in 1985 turned into about €38,000 in 2025. What did almost all the work?
options: Time: 40 years without selling
A single company that shot up
Buying and selling at just the right moment
h1l1-6.explanation: All it took was not touching it for 40 years. There was no need to time when to buy or sell, and the S&P 500 is 500 companies, not just one.

u8l1-1.prompt: You buy an Inditex share. What are you?
options: Co-owner of a tiny part of it
A customer with a discount in all its shops
A lender: the company owes you that money
u8l1-1.explanation: A share is part of the company's capital: you share in its profits and its risks. Lending money to the company would mean buying a bond.

options: inflation
coupons
fees
capital gains
u8l1-3.explanation: You make money from what the company pays out (dividends) and from the rise in price (capital gains). Coupons belong to bonds.

u8l1-7.prompt: If a company goes bust, shareholders get paid before banks and bondholders.
options: True
False
u8l1-7.explanation: They get paid last, after all the creditors, and almost never get anything back.

u8l1-8.prompt: According to Bessembinder (2018), out of some 26,000 US stocks between 1926 and 2016, what share generated all of the market's net gain?
options: Around 4 %
Almost all: most of them made money
Roughly half of them
u8l1-8.explanation: Just 4 % accounted for the entire net gain, and more than half returned less than Treasury bills. That's why a single share is risky and it pays to diversify.

u8l1-11.prompt: Your cousin wants to put all her savings into a single trendy share because «it just keeps going up». What do you advise?
options: All into that share: if it's rising so much, it'll keep rising
Spread it across many companies with a fund
Buy it, but sell as soon as it dips a little
u8l1-11.explanation: A single share can multiply or sink, and very few generate almost all the gains. Spreading across many stops everything depending on just one; the temptation of «if it's rising, it'll keep rising» forgets that it can also fall a long way.
feedback: Having gone up says nothing about what it'll do. Tesla fell as much as 72 %: with everything in it, all her savings fall.
If one company falls, the others cushion the blow: she doesn't depend on picking the exception.
She'll sell at the first normal dip, often at a loss, and still has everything in a single company.

u5l3-1.prompt: The best buying price is €20.10 and the best selling price €20.14. If you buy right now, what price do you pay?
u5l3-1.explanation: You buy at the best selling price (ask): it's what the seller is asking.

u5l3-5.prompt: Put in order what happens when lots of buyers arrive in a hurry.
options: The shares at €10.04 run out
The next purchases are matched at €10.05
The last traded price goes up
Lots of market buy orders arrive
u5l3-5.explanation: That's how the price rises: demand eats through supply step by step.

u5l3-6.prompt: Put a Madrid Stock Exchange session in order.
options: Closing auction (17:30-17:35)
The closing price is published
Market open (9:00-17:30)
Opening auction (8:30-9:00)
u5l3-6.explanation: Two auctions frame the continuous session.

u5l3-8.prompt: What can move a share's price? Select all that apply.
options: The price it floated at years ago
More sellers turning up than buyers
The price you paid when you bought it
The company's results
u5l3-8.explanation: The price is moved by whatever changes what people are willing to pay today: more sellers, results, news. What you paid or the flotation price no longer count.

u5l3-9.prompt: Ana wants to sell 2,000 shares in a small company right now. On the buy side of the book there are 300 at €5.00, 500 at €4.90 and 1,200 at €4.70. What does she do?
options: Places a limit order at €5.00 and sells bit by bit
Sells all 2,000 at market
Sells at market and places more sell orders at the same time, just in case
u5l3-9.explanation: With illiquid securities, a large market order moves the price against you.
feedback: She sells what's there at her price and the rest waits: she doesn't give it away out of impatience.
She eats through the book: she gets €9,590, an average of about €4.80 versus the best price of €5.00.
More selling pressure on a thin book: the price falls even further.

u5l3-11.prompt: Does it push the price up or down?
options: Lots of sellers arrive in a hurry
News comes out that its sales are falling
Lots of buyers arrive in a hurry
The company earns far more than expected
u5l3-11.explanation: The price rises when there's more appetite to buy than to sell, and falls the other way round. Good news attracts buyers; bad news, sellers.

u6l1-1.prompt: Book: best bid €15.20, best ask €15.23. You place a market buy order. What price do you get in at?
u6l1-1.explanation: You buy at the best selling price (ask), the one the seller is asking.

u6l1-2.prompt: In that same book (€15.20 / €15.23), if you sell at market, how much do you get per share?
u6l1-2.explanation: You sell at the best buying price (bid), the one the buyer is paying.

options: Buying right at the open after bombshell news
A heavily traded ETF mid-session
Placing the order on a Saturday for Monday
10 shares of a big IBEX company mid-session
Selling a security that barely trades
u6l1-9.explanation: High liquidity and normal hours: a market order works fine. Low liquidity, the open and news: better to cap the price.

u6l1-10.prompt: Put in order what happens when you place a market buy order.
options: The broker sends the order
You get the confirmation with the execution price
It's matched with the best selling price
You tap «buy at market»
u6l1-10.explanation: You find out the final price at the end, not when you tap.

u19l1-1.prompt: Match each part of the chart with what it shows.
options: Horizontal axis
Vertical axis
Bars at the bottom
Each candle
u19l1-1.explanation: Time runs from left to right, price goes up the side and volume sits underneath. Each candle sums up one period: a minute, a day or a week.

u19l1-2.prompt: Which price in each period is considered the most important?
options: The high of the period
The close
The open of the period
u19l1-2.explanation: The close is the price buyers and sellers settled on at the end of the period. Almost all indicators are calculated using closes.

u19l1-3.prompt: Tap the highest close on this chart (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · June–August 2026)
u19l1-3.explanation: The high came before the end and then the price pulled back a little. The highest point doesn't have to be the last one.

u19l1-4.prompt: Now tap the lowest close (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2025)
u19l1-4.explanation: The low isn't at the end: after touching it, the price bounced. Finding the extremes is the first step in reading a chart.

u19l1-5.prompt: In English, the four prices of each period are summed up as ____.
options: RSI
CPI
ETF
OHLC

u19l1-10.prompt: You run your finger over a candle on the E-Trading chart. What data do you see? Tick all that apply.
options: The close
The reason for the rise or the fall
The high and the low
The dividend it paid that day
u19l1-10.explanation: You see the period's four prices, plus the change and the volume. The chart doesn't tell you why it moved or what the company paid out.

u19l1-11.prompt: Lumi wants to put all her savings into a share that has been rising for three months. What do you reply?
options: The chart says what happened, not what will happen
Yes: if it's risen for three months, it'll most likely keep going
No: if it's risen that much, it's bound to fall
u19l1-11.explanation: A chart is the record of what has already happened. It shows how the price has moved, but it doesn't guarantee what it will do: neither that it keeps rising nor that it falls.
feedback: Exactly. It could carry on or turn around: these are probabilities, not certainties.
Nobody knows. A chart records the past: the rise could end tomorrow.
You don't know that either: the chart doesn't say whether it'll go up or down.
lines: This share has been rising non-stop for three months.
So it's bound to keep going. Shall I put all my savings in?

u1l5-3.prompt: Match each case with the type of interest.
options: You always earn on what you put in
You also earn on what you've already earned
A credit card debt that grows on itself
u1l5-3.explanation: Compounding speeds up growth… including the growth of debts.

u1l5-5.prompt: Compound interest only works in your favour.
options: True
False
u1l5-5.explanation: It works against you too: a revolving credit card at 20 % doubles the debt in under 4 years.

u1l5-10.prompt: Marta is 18 and has €1,000 from a gift. She plans to invest it «when I finish my degree, in 5 years». What do you advise?
options: Start now, even if only with part of it
Wait: at 18 it's still too early to invest
Keep it at home until then
u1l5-10.explanation: Time matters as much as the return: starting 5 years earlier lets compound interest work for 5 more years. Waiting seems prudent, but it has a cost you can't see.
feedback: Every year she waits is one less year of compound interest: the first euros are the ones with the most time to grow.
The opposite: at 18 she has time on her side, which is what matters most.
Under the mattress it doesn't grow, and with prices rising it buys less each year.

options: The curve gets steeper the more time passes
You earn the same in year 1 as in year 30
What you earn is added on and also generates gains
Each year you earn on what you put in at the start
u1l5-11.explanation: With simple interest, each year's gain is always the same. With compound interest, you earn on an ever-bigger base, which is why the later years grow much more than the early ones.

u1l5-12.prompt: Put in order, from least to most, what you'd have after 30 years of setting aside €100 a month.
options: At 2 % a year
At 5 % a year
At 7 % a year
At 0 % a year
u1l5-12.explanation: Roughly €36,000, €49,000, €82,000 and €117,000. You put in the same in all four cases, €36,000: a few points a year change the end result enormously.

u6l1-11.prompt: Mid-session, you place a market order to buy €500 of Apple, one of the most traded companies in the world. What do you expect?
options: To get in almost at the price you see on screen
To get in at exactly the price you see, guaranteed
To pay quite a bit more than you see
u6l1-11.explanation: With lots of people buying and selling at once, there's always someone on the other side at almost the same price. A market order gets expensive when there are few sellers, not with a big company mid-session.
feedback: That's it: with heavily traded companies during normal hours, the difference is usually a few cents.
A market order guarantees that it gets filled, not the exact price: it can vary a little.
That happens with thinly traded stocks, at the open or right after news, not here.

u6l1-12.prompt: It's Saturday and you place a market buy order for a Spanish share. What happens?
options: It waits and is filled on Monday at the open
It's filled right away, at Friday's last price, the one you see
It cancels itself because it's the weekend
u6l1-12.explanation: With the market closed, a market order is filled at the open, at whatever price comes out then. If news breaks over the weekend, the price can jump: «now» doesn't mean «at this price».
feedback: That's it: with the market closed, the order waits. Monday's price may differ from today's.
With the market closed there's nobody to match it with: it waits until it opens.
It doesn't cancel: it stays pending until the market opens.

u8l1-12.prompt: Tesla doesn't pay dividends. Your cousin says that means its shares are no good for making money. What do you tell him?
options: That he's right: without dividends you make nothing
That you also make money if the price goes up
That the company will give him his money back on a set date
u8l1-12.explanation: With a share you make money in two ways: dividends and capital growth, the rise in the price. Without dividends, everything depends on the price, which can rise and can also fall.
feedback: You can make money from the price rising. Anyone who bought Tesla at the end of 2018 multiplied their money without a single dividend.
That's it: without dividends, what you make or lose depends on how much the price goes up or down.
That's a bond. A share has no repayment date: you win or lose depending on its price.
